title: Multi-cluster backstop and capacity-stitch runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose: This doc is a working draft for a fast, low-friction response when a zone/cluster experiences degraded GPU capacity (hardware failure, thermal trips, or mass node flake). Goal is to provide a predictable path to keep latency SLOs for critical tenants by stitching capacity across clusters and performing a safe physical GPU/cartridge replacement flow while minimizing blast radius.

Scope: node cordon/drain, temporary capacity injection across clusters, prioritized pod rescheduling, physical GPU replacement checklist, rollback, and post-incident simulation notes. This is not the full procurement or long-term capacity planning doc — it's an operational playbook for the first 3 hours.

Quick triage (first 10 minutes):
- Confirm alert source and scope: NOC -> PagerDuty -> #sre-incident Slack channel.
- Identify impacted pool(s): check metrics dashboard (Console > Per-route > capacity) + cluster-health panel.
- Verify whether degradation is due to GPU hardware (thermal/trip), kernel/OOM, or networking. Look at node exporter, nvidia-smi, and dmesg.
- Triage commands:
  - kubectl get nodes -l pool=gpu -o wide
  - kubectl describe node <node-name> | egrep -i "OutOfMemory|Fail|gpu|nvidia"
  - ssh ops@<node> sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager | tail -n 50
  - ssh ops@<node> sudo nvidia-smi -q || echo 'nvidia-smi failed'

If hardware fault suspected (GPU shows ECC errors, thermal trip, or is unresponsive):
- Immediately cordon the node to prevent new pods: kubectl cordon <node>
- Drain non-critical pods with conservative evict timeouts: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
- If drain stalls, inspect pending pods: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> and check PodDisruptionBudget for the namespace. If PDB blocks critical system pods, escalate to on-call SRE lead.

Capacity-stitch strategy (short-term capacity rebalancing):
1) Evaluate remaining capacity in same zone cluster and sibling clusters (in same region). Use console capacity panel and cluster metrics.
2) If sibling cluster has warm spare nodes, update routing policy to route a percentage of traffic there as a temporary backstop:
   - Update smart routing policy in control-plane: PATCH /routing/policies/<policy-id> set fallback_clusters = [cluster-b]
   - If no control-plane change is available, fallback to DNS weight changes via the load-balancer (coord with network infra).
3) If no warm spare is available, trigger ephemeral capacity injection: spin up pre-configured preemptible GPU nodes in a cold cluster (runbook automation):
   - run: ./ops/capacity/stitch-start --region us-west2 --cluster cluster-c --count 4 --gpu-type a100-80gb --tags temporary-backstop
   - Confirm nodes join via: kubectl get nodes -l temp-backstop=true -o wide
4) Prioritize scheduling: update cluster-scheduler hinting (labels/taints) to prefer critical workloads to the new nodes. Example taint: kubectl taint nodes <node> temporary-backstop=true:NoExecute (then use tolerations on critical DaemonSet/pods).

Physical GPU replacement (if node is physically failed):
- Safety first: coordinate with on-call hardware tech. Ensure power off and ESD precautions.
- Replacement checklist:
  1) Confirm device ID and inventory tag of the failed GPU.
  2) Document current node state and captured logs (nvidia-smi -q, /var/log/messages, dmesg). Upload to incident folder.
  3) Cordon node (should already be cordoned). Confirm pods are evacuated.
  4) Power down node via BMC: ipmitool -I lanplus -H <bmc> -U <user> -P <pass> chassis power off
  5) Physically swap GPU cartridge using approved torque specs and connectors. Re-seat power and SFF connectors.
  6) Power on node; watch POST and OS boot via BMC console.
  7) Verify GPU presence: sudo nvidia-smi -q; check for ECC errors cleared.
  8) Run health-check script: /opt/infra/bin/gpu-healthcheck --full. If pass, remove cordon: kubectl uncordon <node> and allow kubelet to accept pods.
- If replacement fails or new card shows errors, mark node for deeper hardware investigation and move remaining capacity add plan.

Safe rollout back into fleet:
- Don't immediately run large-scale scheduling onto the node. Apply a graduated drain/unlabel process: add label: gpu-ready=probation and set scheduler weight low. Monitor GPU and thermal graphs for 30–60 minutes.
- If anomalies observed, cordon again and revert to spare capacity.

Rollback and fallback:
- If capacity-stitching automation causes higher latency (regression > 5% p50), revert routing weights and decommission ephemeral nodes: ./ops/capacity/stitch-stop --tag temporary-backstop
- If model-serving pods are failing due to CPU/GPU architecture mismatch, revert to previous node selectors and redeploy model variant for compatibility.

Observability and signals to monitor during incident:
- token-latency-per-route p50/p95/p99
- cpu/gpu utilization and GPU memory alloc failures
- OOMKilled pod counts by namespace
- scheduling failure rates and pending pods by reason
- kube-controller errors in control-plane
- BMC/host power cycle logs

Simulation / DR drill notes (to run weekly before high-load events):
- Run a controlled GPU-cartridge-failure simulation by cordoning + synthetic thermal trip via workload injector (use a reserved test cluster).
- Steps: 1) cordon 2) drain 3) trigger routing weight shift 4) bring ephemeral nodes 5) validate latency 6) revert. Document timings.
- Metrics to record: time-to-cordon, time-to-evacuate, time-to-ephemeral-join, SLO delta during event.

Open questions / TODOs:
- TODO: define RBAC for the capacity-stitch automation so only SRE-runbook bots can spin ephemeral nodes. Owner: Miguel.
- TODO: add automation to auto-create incident folders and attach logs automatically to JIRA ticket. Owner: Evelyn.
- Question: should we prefer preemptible vs on-demand ephemeral nodes for speed vs stability? Need cost/latency analysis.

Notes and references:
- Slack: #sre-incident, #infra-ops. Use /incident create to generate PG template.
- GitHub infra PR for automation: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-ops/pull/782
- Related JIRA: JIRA-SRE-891 (capacity stitch prototype).

Post-incident checklist (within 24h):
- Capture root cause and timeline in the incident doc.
- Runpostmortem template and link to JIRA.
- Verify inventory replacement recorded in CMDB and update spare count.
- Schedule a simulation to exercise same failure mode in staging within 7 days.

Appendix: quick commands cheat-sheet:
- cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
- drain (safe): kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
- uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node>
- list temp nodes: kubectl get nodes -l temp-backstop=true -o wide
- tear down ephemeral capacity: ./ops/capacity/stitch-stop --tag temporary-backstop

End of draft. This is intentionally concise and focused on practical operator steps. Feedback requested: where should automation run (control-plane vs infra-ops CLI) and approval flow for spinning ephemeral nodes during a Sev2?
